prompt: Put the lesson's three questions before a promotion in order.
hint: Alive, then data, then a second promotion.
items: How much does the standby have?
Will anything promote a second time?
trap: Asking about data before knowing the primary is gone can promote beside a live primary.

prompt: You cannot connect to the primary from your laptop. What does that tell you?

choices.text: The primary has crashed
choices.why: It may be alive and taking writes from whoever can reach it.

choices.text: The standby has every write
choices.why: Your laptop's connection says nothing about the standby.

choices.text: The path from you is broken
choices.why: Right: it is a fact about the path, not the primary.

choices.text: It is safe to promote at once
choices.why: Promoting beside a live primary makes two primaries.

prompt: Match each term with what it means.

pairs.right: Promoting a standby because the primary failed
Moving the primary's role on purpose, to a standby
The command that turns a standby into a primary

right_distractors: Restoring a backup onto a new server

prompt: How did the lesson crash the primary?

choices.text: kill -9 on its postmaster
choices.why: Right: the first line of postmaster.pid, killed without a chance to shut down.

choices.text: pg_ctlcluster stop -m fast
choices.why: That is a clean shutdown, with a checkpoint.

choices.text: Deleting the data directory
choices.why: That is lesson 1's disaster, not a crash.

choices.text: Unplugging the network cable
choices.why: A single machine has no cable between its servers.

prompt: The standby's received and replayed positions are equal after the crash. What can it not tell you?

choices.text: Whether it is still in recovery
choices.why: pg_is_in_recovery() answered that.

choices.text: Its last order id
choices.why: It showed 50001.

choices.text: Which timeline it is on
choices.why: That is in its control file.

choices.text: Whether the primary wrote more it never got
choices.why: Right: an asynchronous standby knows what it has, never what it missed.

prompt: After `promote`, `pg_control_checkpoint()` showed the new primary on ___ 2.
The last order before the crash was 50001 and the first after the promotion was 50034. How many ids were skipped?
Why did order ids jump after the promotion?
hint: How does a sequence write its values to the log?

choices.text: The standby's sequence restarted
choices.why: It continued past the old primary's, not from 1.

choices.text: Logged ahead in batches
choices.why: Right: sequences log values 32 at a time; the standby replayed the batch, not the last value handed out.

choices.text: Rows were lost in the crash
choices.why: The ids skip even when nothing is lost.

choices.text: Promotion rounds ids to a multiple of 32
choices.why: There is no rounding; the next unlogged batch starts there.

prompt: The old primary rebooted after the failover. What did it do?
hint: Its data directory says nothing happened.

choices.text: Started as a standby of the new primary
choices.why: It has no standby.signal, so nothing makes it a standby.

choices.text: Started as a primary and took a write
choices.why: Right: two primaries, and the same id for two customers.

choices.text: Refused to start, seeing a newer timeline
choices.why: It never looks at the other server.

choices.text: Started read-only until an operator decides
choices.why: Nothing in PostgreSQL does that.

prompt: What rule does split-brain after a reboot lead to?

choices.text: Never promote a standby
choices.why: Promotion is the point; the risk is a second primary.

choices.text: Always rebuild every standby
choices.why: That is about rejoining, not about the old primary.

choices.text: Use synchronous replication
choices.why: That decides what is lost, not how many primaries exist.

choices.text: It never returns as a primary
choices.why: Right: kept down, or brought back as a standby.

prompt: Why is a script on the standby that promotes when the primary stops answering unsafe?
hint: What does it see when the network between them breaks?

choices.text: It promotes beside a live, cut-off primary
choices.why: Right: the same picture as the reboot, with no reboot needed.

choices.text: Scripts cannot run pg_ctlcluster
choices.why: They can.

choices.text: It promotes too slowly to matter
choices.why: Speed is not the problem; the decision is.

choices.text: The standby has no way to reach the primary
choices.why: It has one, and that is the only way it decides.

prompt: Why did `pg_rewind` refuse the first time?

choices.text: The old primary was still running
choices.why: It was stopped first.

choices.text: The new primary was on another timeline
choices.why: That is what pg_rewind exists to handle.

choices.text: Neither wal_log_hints nor checksums was on
choices.why: Right: without them, hint-bit changes leave no trace in the log.

choices.text: It needs the archive
choices.why: It reads the target's own log.

prompt: When must `wal_log_hints` be turned on to help with a failover?
hint: It needs a restart, and it describes the log being written.

choices.text: Right after the failure, before the rewind
choices.why: The divergent changes were already written without it.

choices.text: On the new primary only
choices.why: The old primary's log is the one read, and either may be old next time.

choices.text: Never; it is only for checksums
choices.why: It is an alternative to checksums.

choices.text: Before the failure, with a restart
choices.why: Right: it only makes the log it writes from then on usable for a rewind.

prompt: `ALTER SYSTEM SET wal_log_hints = on` on the 5434 left the 5432 at `off`. Why?

choices.text: The 5432 had not been restarted
choices.why: It had been.

choices.text: Standbys ignore wal_log_hints
choices.why: It was set on the 5432 next and took effect.

choices.text: auto.conf is not replicated
choices.why: Right: ALTER SYSTEM writes a file replication does not copy; postgresql.auto.conf is each server's own.

choices.text: The setting needs a reload, not a restart
choices.why: It needs a restart, and was given one.

prompt: What does a clean shutdown of a primary do that a crash does not?

choices.text: Writes a final checkpoint
choices.why: Right: a shutdown checkpoint, and it waits until standbys receive the log up to it, so nothing is lost.

choices.text: Deletes its replication slots
choices.why: Slots survive a shutdown.

choices.text: Promotes the standby itself
choices.why: Promotion is always an explicit act.

choices.text: Copies the archive to the standby
choices.why: Streaming carries the log; the archive is not involved.

prompt: The stopped primary's last checkpoint starts at `0/6000110`; the standby replayed to `0/6000188`. How many bytes past the start of that record is the standby (hex 188 minus 110)?
Put the switchover's steps in order.
hint: Clean stop first; the application moves last.
items: Confirm the standby replayed past its last checkpoint
Make the old primary a standby and start it
Point the application at the new primary
trap: Promoting before the check risks the switchover becoming a failover with loss.

prompt: Why did the old primary need only `standby.signal` and a slot to become a standby?
hint: What was still in its postgresql.auto.conf?

choices.text: pg_ctlcluster rewrote its configuration
choices.why: Nothing rewrote it.

choices.text: Its old primary_conninfo was still there
choices.why: Right: written by pg_basebackup -R and ignored while it was a primary.

choices.text: A switchover copies settings automatically
choices.why: Nothing copies settings between servers.

choices.text: Standbys need no connection settings
choices.why: They need primary_conninfo to stream.

prompt: Why does `pg_rewind` need `--config-file` on Ubuntu?

choices.text: To read the source server's password
choices.why: The password comes from the connection, not the config.

choices.text: It writes the new primary_conninfo there
choices.why: That goes into postgresql.auto.conf.

choices.text: postgresql.conf lives in /etc/postgresql
choices.why: Right: its single-user crash recovery could not find it otherwise.

choices.text: Ubuntu disables pg_rewind without it
choices.why: It ran, and failed at its first step.

prompt: After the rewind, the old primary did not stream: `replication slot "standby1" does not exist`. Where did that name come from?

choices.text: The 5434's postgresql.auto.conf
choices.why: Right: copied over by pg_rewind, it carried the 5434's old primary_slot_name.

choices.text: pg_rewind invents a slot name
choices.why: It wrote no slot name at all.

choices.text: The new primary's pg_hba.conf
choices.why: pg_hba.conf has no slot names.

choices.text: It is the default slot name
choices.why: There is no default.

prompt: When is a failover finished?
hint: Not when the new primary takes writes.

choices.text: When the new primary accepts its first write
choices.why: The old primary may still come back as a primary, or never return.

choices.text: When pg_rewind prints Done!
choices.why: It printed Done! and the standby still did not stream.

choices.text: When the incident report is written
choices.why: That is lesson 22, after the failover.

choices.text: When the old primary streams again as a standby
choices.why: Right: that is the check to end every failover on.

prompt: With a synchronous standby (lesson 12), which of the three questions does a failover no longer need to ask?
hint: What does a synchronous standby guarantee it has?

choices.text: Is the primary really gone?
choices.why: Synchronous replication says nothing about the primary's state.

choices.text: How much does the standby have?
choices.why: Right: every confirmed commit is on it, so nothing confirmed is lost.

choices.text: Will anything promote a second time?
choices.why: Split-brain is as possible as ever.

choices.text: None; all three remain the same
choices.why: One of them is answered by the configuration.
